questions.lo: Energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)
questions.q: Steam from a kettle condenses into water on a cold window. What happens to energy as the steam condenses?
options: The steam takes in energy from the window
No energy moves, as it is just water
Cold flows from the glass to the steam
The steam gives out energy to the window
questions.explain: Yes. Condensing gives energy out: as the steam turns into water, energy is transferred from it to the colder window.
optionWhy: You may have thought the steam takes in energy as it condenses. In fact condensing is the reverse of boiling: boiling takes energy in, so condensing gives energy out.
You may have thought no energy moves because no new substance forms. In fact a change of state still transfers energy: condensing steam gives energy out.
You may have thought cold flows from the window into the steam. In fact cold is not a thing that moves; energy moves from the hotter steam to the colder window.
Yes. Condensing gives energy out: as the steam turns into water, energy is transferred from it to the colder window.

questions.lo: Energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)
questions.q: Pure water is boiling in a pan, and the hob stays on. What happens to the water's temperature while it boils?
options: It stays at its boiling point
It keeps rising as it is heated
It falls as heat leaves in bubbles
It falls as the energy is used up
questions.explain: Yes. While pure water boils, its temperature stays at its boiling point (100 °C at normal air pressure). The energy from the hob turns more water into steam.
optionWhy: Yes. While pure water boils, its temperature stays at its boiling point (100 °C at normal air pressure). The energy from the hob turns more water into steam.
You may have thought heating always makes the temperature rise. In fact, while water boils, the energy changes liquid into steam and the temperature stays at the boiling point.
You may have thought the bubbles are made of heat. In fact they are water vapour; heat is not a substance, and the temperature stays at the boiling point.
You may have thought energy gets used up as water boils. In fact energy is never destroyed: it changes the water into steam, and the temperature stays the same.

questions.lo: Energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)
questions.q: The diagram shows the particles of a pure substance before and after a change of state. What must happen for this change to take place?
options: Energy must leave as the particles break free
Energy must be transferred to the substance
Its temperature must rise as the change happens
None is needed, as no new substance forms
questions.explain: Yes. The particles go from neat rows to a jumbled heap, so the solid has melted. Melting happens only when energy is transferred to the substance.
optionWhy: You may have thought particles give out energy as they break out of their rows. In fact particles need energy to move apart, so melting takes energy in.
Yes. The particles go from neat rows to a jumbled heap, so the solid has melted. Melting happens only when energy is transferred to the substance.
You may have thought the temperature rises all through melting. In fact a pure substance stays at its melting point until it has all melted, even though energy keeps going in.
You may have thought no energy is involved because no new substance forms. In fact melting is a physical change that still takes energy in.

questions.lo: Energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)
questions.q: The graph shows the temperature of a pure solid heated steadily. It melts between P and Q. What is true between P and Q?
options: It takes in no energy, as its temperature is steady
It gives out energy, as its particles break away
It takes in energy, which changes its state
It uses up energy, which then no longer exists
questions.explain: Yes. Between P and Q the heater keeps transferring energy to the substance, but the energy changes solid into liquid instead of raising the temperature. That is why the line is flat.
optionWhy: You may have thought a steady temperature means no energy is going in. In fact the heater is still on and the substance keeps taking in energy; the energy melts the solid.
You may have thought melting gives out energy as particles break away. In fact particles need energy to move apart, so melting takes energy in.
Yes. Between P and Q the heater keeps transferring energy to the substance, but the energy changes solid into liquid instead of raising the temperature. That is why the line is flat.
You may have thought the energy is used up and gone. In fact energy is never destroyed: between P and Q it is changing the solid into a liquid.

questions.lo: Energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)
questions.q: On a cool, cloudy day a puddle slowly dries up. No heater or sunshine warms it. What happens to energy as the water evaporates?
options: Energy is taken in from the surroundings
None is needed, as nothing hot is near it
It is given out as the particles escape
Cold goes into the water from the cool air
questions.explain: Yes. Evaporation always takes in energy. With no heater or sunshine, the energy comes from the surroundings: the ground and the air.
optionWhy: Yes. Evaporation always takes in energy. With no heater or sunshine, the energy comes from the surroundings: the ground and the air.
You may have thought evaporation needs something hot. In fact all evaporation takes in energy; here it comes from the ground and air around the puddle.
You may have thought escaping particles give energy out. In fact particles need energy to break away from the liquid, so evaporation takes energy in.
You may have thought cold flows into the water from the cool air. In fact cold is not a thing that moves; evaporating water takes in energy from its surroundings.

questions.lo: Energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)
questions.q: Pure iron melts and freezes at 1538 °C. Liquid iron poured into a mould turns solid at this temperature. What happens to energy?
options: It is taken in from the mould and from the air
None, as nothing can freeze when that hot
It is used up as the liquid iron sets
It is given out to the mould and the air
questions.explain: Yes. Liquid iron turning solid is freezing, and freezing gives out energy. The energy is transferred to the colder mould and air.
optionWhy: You may have thought turning solid takes energy in. In fact freezing is the reverse of melting: melting takes energy in, so freezing gives it out.
You may have thought freezing only happens when things are cold. In fact every liquid has its own freezing point, and iron's is 1538 °C; it gives out energy as it freezes.
You may have thought energy gets used up as the iron sets. In fact energy is never destroyed: it is transferred from the iron to the mould and the air.
Yes. Liquid iron turning solid is freezing, and freezing gives out energy. The energy is transferred to the colder mould and air.

questions.q: What happens in an endothermic reaction?
options: Energy is given out to the surroundings
Cold is given out to the surroundings
Energy is taken in from the surroundings
Energy is used up and then destroyed
questions.explain: Yes. In an endothermic reaction energy is transferred from the surroundings into the reacting chemicals, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
optionWhy: You may have mixed up the two words. Energy given out means exothermic ('exo' = exit); endothermic means energy goes in.
You may have thought the reaction gives out cold, because it feels cold. In fact it takes energy in from your hand and the air; cold is not a thing that moves.
Yes. In an endothermic reaction energy is transferred from the surroundings into the reacting chemicals, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
You may have thought energy is used up in the reaction. In fact energy is never destroyed; it is taken in by the chemicals from the surroundings.

questions.q: The diagram shows a thermometer in citric acid solution before and after adding sodium hydrogencarbonate (bicarbonate of soda). What does it show about the reaction, and why?
options: Exothermic: the chemicals gave out their energy
Endothermic: it took in energy from the surroundings
Endothermic: it gave cold out to the surroundings
Exothermic: every reaction gives out some energy
questions.explain: Yes. The reading fell from 20 °C to 14 °C, so the solution lost energy to the reacting chemicals. A fall in the temperature of the surroundings shows an endothermic reaction.
optionWhy: You may have thought the falling reading shows the chemicals giving out energy. In fact the thermometer measures the surroundings: they got colder because the chemicals took energy in from them.
Yes. The reading fell from 20 °C to 14 °C, so the solution lost energy to the reacting chemicals. A fall in the temperature of the surroundings shows an endothermic reaction.
You may have thought cold was given out. In fact cold is not a thing that moves; energy moved from the solution into the reacting chemicals.
You may have thought every reaction gives out energy. In fact some reactions take energy in; here the temperature fell, so the reaction is endothermic.

questions.q: Which of these is an endothermic chemical reaction?
options: Ice melting into water in a warm drink
A candle burning once a match lights it
Hydrochloric acid neutralising an alkali
Heating calcium carbonate until it breaks down
questions.explain: Yes. Heating calcium carbonate until it breaks down is thermal decomposition, which is endothermic: the calcium carbonate takes in energy from the flame as it breaks down into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
optionWhy: You may have thought melting is a reaction because it takes in energy. In fact no new substance is made: melting is a physical change, not a chemical reaction.
You may have thought burning is endothermic because it needs a match to start. In fact, once lit, the candle gives out energy and keeps burning, so it is exothermic.
You may have mixed up the two words. Neutralisation warms the solution, so it gives energy out: it is exothermic, not endothermic.

Yes. Heating calcium carbonate until it breaks down is thermal decomposition, which is endothermic: the calcium carbonate takes in energy from the flame as it breaks down into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: A hand warmer contains iron powder. When it is opened, the iron reacts with oxygen in the air and the pack warms up. Which is correct?
options: Exothermic: it creates new energy from nothing
Exothermic: it transfers energy to your hands
Endothermic: it takes in energy and heats up
Endothermic: it warms the things around it
questions.explain: Yes. The iron reacting with oxygen gives out energy, which is transferred to the pack and your hands. A reaction that warms its surroundings is exothermic.
optionWhy: You may have thought the reaction makes energy. In fact energy cannot be created; it is transferred from the reacting iron and oxygen to your hands.
Yes. The iron reacting with oxygen gives out energy, which is transferred to the pack and your hands. A reaction that warms its surroundings is exothermic.
You may have thought taking energy in makes the pack hot. In fact a reaction that takes energy in makes its surroundings colder; the pack warms because the reaction gives energy out.
You may have mixed up the two words. A reaction that warms its surroundings is exothermic ('exo' = exit); endothermic reactions make their surroundings colder.

questions.q: A gas fire needs a spark to light it. Then it keeps burning by itself and warms the room. What type of reaction is the burning, and why?
options: Exothermic: once lit, it gives energy to the room
Endothermic: it needs energy from a spark to start
Exothermic: it passes on the spark's energy
Endothermic: it gives out energy to the room
questions.explain: Yes. The spark only starts the reaction. Once lit, burning gives out far more energy than the spark supplied and keeps going by itself, so it is exothermic.
optionWhy: Yes. The spark only starts the reaction. Once lit, burning gives out far more energy than the spark supplied and keeps going by itself, so it is exothermic.
You may have thought needing a spark makes it endothermic. In fact, once lit, this fire keeps burning by itself and gives out far more energy than the spark supplied, so it is exothermic.
You may have thought the energy comes from the spark. In fact a tiny spark could not warm a room; the energy comes from the gas and oxygen as they react.
You may have mixed up the two words. A reaction that gives energy out to the room is exothermic ('exo' = exit), not endothermic.

questions.q: Which of these is an exothermic chemical reaction?
options: Steam condensing on a cold window
Heating copper carbonate in a flame
Respiration in your muscle cells
Citric acid with bicarbonate of soda
questions.explain: Yes. Respiration is a chemical reaction in cells that gives out energy, which keeps your body warm and lets your muscles work.

You may have thought the reaction gives out heat because the tube gets hot. In fact the heat comes from the Bunsen burner; breaking down copper carbonate takes energy in, so the reaction is endothermic.
